title: 3 AI myths that need busting
author: Paul Matthews
summary: Paul Matthews addresses three myths that cloud teachers' thinking about AI in schools. First, that it is hypocritical to use AI while telling students not to: he argues teachers and students have different goals, so a tool can help a teacher facilitate learning without helping a student learn. Second, that AI is only for tech enthusiasts: he says he is an impact enthusiast, and that an hour or two of training lets any teacher create more tailored, feedback-rich environments. Third, that AI demands radical new classroom practice: he says it should be used to do proven basics, such as text differentiation, task-specific rubrics and retrieval practice quizzes, more often for more learners. The piece opens with a PD promotion and is a short opinion essay, but its three claims are clear and school-specific.
points: Teacher and student AI use are not symmetrical, because teachers aim to facilitate learning while students aim to learn.
Enthusiasm for AI should rest on classroom impact rather than on love of technology.
AI is best used to do evidence-based basics more often for more learners, not to replace the teacher's repertoire.
Concrete uses named are text differentiation, task-specific rubrics, differentiated teaching and retrieval practice quizzes.
quotes: Teachers and students have two fundamentally different goals. The teacher is there to facilitate learning. The student is there to learn.

You can use AI to do more evidence-based practices more often for more learners (I’ve just written on using AI for text differentiation and retrieval practice, for example). There’s a clear benefit to your students. If we open up student use without thought, however, the benefit is not so clear.
With only an hour or two of training, every teacher can use AI to put their students in a more tailored, personalised, feedback-rich environment than ever before.
It’s easy to think that if we start using new technology we have to throw that bag in the bin. Many teachers recoil from this. I don’t blame them. No one wants to start over.
Instead of using new tech to do new things, we can use new technology to do the basics better. We can use AI to do the things we know work, more often, for more learners.
